title: TypeScript: generics & utility types
summary: Generic functions and constraints, keyof and indexed access types, the utility types you use daily (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Readonly, ReturnType, Awaited), and deriving types instead of repeating them.
lesson:
## Generics: types as parameters

```ts
function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined { return xs[0]; }
first([1, 2])        // T inferred as number: returns number | undefined
first(['a'])         // string | undefined
```

A generic keeps the relationship between input and output. Without it you would write `any[] => any` and lose every check downstream. Inference does the work in most calls: `first([1, 2])` needs no `<number>`. Write the type argument only when there is nothing to infer from, as in `new Map<string, User>()` or `useState<User | null>(null)`.

**Constraints** say what a type parameter must have:

```ts
function byId<T extends { id: string }>(xs: T[], id: string): T | undefined {
  return xs.find((x) => x.id === id);   // x.id is allowed because of the constraint
}
byId([{ id: 1 }], '1');   // error: number is not assignable to string
```

## keyof and indexed access

```ts
type Keys = keyof { a: 1; b: 2 };           // 'a' | 'b'
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] { return obj[key]; }
get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'name')            // string
get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'nope')            // error
```

`T[K]` (indexed access) is "the type of property K of T".

`K extends keyof T` limits `key` to names that exist on the object, so a typo like `'nmae'` is a compile error instead of an `undefined` at runtime. The return type follows the key: `get(row, 'id')` is a number and `get(row, 'name')` a string, from one function and no overloads.

## The utility types

```ts
interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; passwordHash: string }

Partial<User>                  // every property optional: PATCH bodies
Required<T>                    // every property required
Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>      // only those keys
Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>     // everything except: public DTOs
Record<'draft' | 'live', number>  // an object with exactly those keys
Readonly<User>                 // assignments to properties are errors
ReturnType<typeof makeUser>    // the return type of a function
Awaited<Promise<Promise<string>>> // string: unwraps promises, recursively
NonNullable<string | null | undefined> // string
```

These are all compile-time only. `Readonly` does not freeze anything at runtime, and `Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>` does not remove the field from an object you send: you still have to build the DTO without it (`const { passwordHash, ...publicUser } = user`). A concrete trap: a handler declared as `(): Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>` that does `return user` compiles, because a value with more properties is assignable to the smaller type.

## Derive types instead of repeating them

Keep one source of truth and derive the rest:

```ts
const ROLES = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer'] as const;
type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];            // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'

type CreateUser = Omit<User, 'id'>;            // POST body
type UpdateUser = Partial<CreateUser>;         // PATCH body
type UserRow = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof db.users.findFirst>>;
```

Change `User` once and every derived type follows. Add `'auditor'` to `ROLES` and `Role` gains it, so every `switch` over a role with a `never` check stops compiling until it handles the new value. A hand-written union kept next to the array drifts away from it silently.

## Mapped and conditional types (reading level)

`Partial` is itself a mapped type: `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`. Conditional types branch on types: `T extends string ? 'text' : 'other'`. You will read them in library typings more than you write them. A conditional type applied to a union checks each member separately: `T extends null ? never : T` turns `string | null` into `string`.

## Where generics show up in CRUD code

A typed API client `get<T>(url): Promise<T>` (remember: the `T` is an unchecked claim about the response, not a validation), repository interfaces `Repo<T extends { id: string }>`, React components `<Select<T> items={T[]} />`, and `Result<T, E>` unions for error handling. In each case one type parameter ties several signatures together, so a change to `T` is checked everywhere it flows.

quiz.prompt: For `function pair<T>(x: T): [T, T]`, what is the type of `pair(5)`?
quiz.explanation: T is inferred from the argument and the literal 5 widens to number, so the result is the tuple `[number, number]`; the signature keeps both the tuple shape and the link to T. `[5, 5]` would need a `const T` type parameter or an `as const` argument.

quiz.prompt: Why does `byId([{ id: 1 }], "1")` fail for `byId<T extends { id: string }>`?
choices: T cannot be inferred from an array of object literals
Generic functions cannot take array parameters
The element's id is a number, violating the constraint
The second argument "1" must be a number like the id
quiz.explanation: The constraint says every T must have a string id, and `{ id: 1 }` has a number id, so the argument does not satisfy `T extends { id: string }`. Inference from object literals works fine, and the "1" argument is not what fails: the element type is.

keyof gives the union of an object type's property NAMES, so it is `'a' | 'b'`. The values 1 | 2 would be `T[keyof T]`, and keyof never produces a tuple; `string` is what keyof gives for a type with a string index signature.

quiz.prompt: Which utility type best describes a PATCH body where any field may be sent?
quiz.explanation: A PATCH body may contain any subset of fields, and `Partial<User>` makes every property optional. Required makes them all mandatory, Pick<User, "id"> keeps only the id, and Readonly forbids assignment without making anything optional.

quiz.prompt: A `Record<"a" | "b", number>` is assigned `{ a: 1 }`. Result?
choices: A runtime error when b is read
quiz.explanation: `Record<K, V>` is the mapped type `{ [P in K]: V }`, so every member of the key union becomes a required property. The literal has no `b`, and tsc rejects the assignment. Keys are not optional unless you wrap the Record in `Partial`, and TypeScript never fills in a default such as 0: types emit no code, so the check happens at compile time, not when b is read.

quiz.prompt: `res.json(user as Omit<User, "passwordHash">)` — is the hash removed from the response?
choices: Yes: Omit removes the field when the object is serialised
Yes in strict mode, where Omit is enforced at runtime
No: types are erased; the object still contains the field
Yes, if passwordHash is declared as an optional field
quiz.explanation: `as Omit<User, "passwordHash">` only changes what the compiler believes about the value. The emitted JavaScript is `res.json(user)`, and `JSON.stringify` writes every own enumerable property, the hash included. No strict mode setting or optional modifier changes that, because no type survives compilation. Remove the field from the data: `const { passwordHash, ...publicUser } = user;`, then send `publicUser`, or map the row to a DTO.

Awaited distributes over a union and unwraps each promise member, while non-promise members pass through: `await` on a string gives the string. So the result is `string | number`, not `number` alone and not still a promise type.

quiz.prompt: `const ROLES = ["admin", "viewer"] as const; type Role = (typeof ROLES)[number];` What is Role?
quiz.explanation: `as const` gives `ROLES` the type `readonly ['admin', 'viewer']`, a tuple whose elements keep their literal types. Indexing an array or tuple type with `number` asks for the type of any element, which for this tuple is the union of its two literals. Without `as const` the array would be `string[]` and Role would widen to `string`; the readonly tuple is the type of ROLES itself, not of one element.

quiz.prompt: Does `Readonly<User>` stop a property from being changed at runtime?
choices: Yes: strict mode throws on writes
Yes, for nested objects as well
No: it is a compile-time check only
quiz.explanation: `Readonly<User>` marks every property `readonly`, and that modifier lives only in the type: tsc reports an assignment as an error and emits the same JavaScript as before. Nothing calls `Object.freeze`, so code that goes around the type, through `as any` or plain JavaScript, can still write. It is also shallow: nested objects stay writable even in the type. Freeze the object when you need a runtime guarantee.

quiz.prompt: In `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, what does `T[K]` mean?
choices: An array of T values indexed by K
The type of property K of T
A tuple of T and K
Either the type K or the type T
quiz.explanation: An indexed access type looks up a property's type the way `obj[key]` looks up a value. With `K extends keyof T`, the call `get({ id: 1, name: 'x' }, 'name')` infers K as `'name'` and returns `string`, while the key `'id'` returns `number`. No array, tuple or either-or union is involved; the point is that the return type follows the key you pass.

flashcards.front: Why use a generic instead of any?
flashcards.back: A generic keeps the link between input and output types, so callers get precise types back; any discards checking everywhere it flows.

flashcards.front: What does a constraint like T extends { id: string } do?
flashcards.back: It limits which types may be used for T and lets the function body use the members the constraint guarantees.
Make every property optional, make every property mandatory, and forbid assignment to properties, all at compile time.
Pick keeps only the named keys; Omit keeps all keys except the named ones.
An object type with exactly the keys in K, each holding a V; with a union of literal keys, every key is required.
ReturnType reads a function's return type; wrapping it in Awaited unwraps the promise an async function returns.

flashcards.front: Do utility types change runtime objects?
flashcards.back: Never. An Omit type does not remove a field from the data; you still have to build the object without it.

flashcards.front: How do you turn a constant list into a union type?
flashcards.back: Declare the array with as const and index its type with number to get the union of its literal elements.

drills.title: pick and omit: the runtime half of Pick and Omit
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We typed the response as `Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>` and the hash still leaked. Write the helpers that actually build the DTO."

**Why it matters.** Utility types are erased. The value you send is whatever object you build, so DTOs need runtime helpers that copy exactly the allowed keys.

**Your task.** Export two functions; both return a NEW object and never modify `obj`:
- `pick(obj, keys)`: only the listed keys that are OWN properties of `obj` (a listed key that is missing is simply absent from the result)
- `omit(obj, keys)`: every own enumerable property of `obj` except the listed keys

`keys` is an array of strings. Inherited properties are never copied by either function.

**Worked example.** `omit({ id: '1', name: 'Ana', passwordHash: 'x' }, ['passwordHash'])` is `{ id: '1', name: 'Ana' }`.

tests.name: omit removes the secret
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.omit, 'function', 'export omit');
assert.deepEqual(mod.omit({ id: '1', name: 'Ana', passwordHash: 'x' }, ['passwordHash']), { id: '1', name: 'Ana' });

tests.name: pick keeps only the listed keys
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.pick, 'function', 'export pick');
assert.deepEqual(mod.pick({ id: '1', name: 'Ana', passwordHash: 'x' }, ['id', 'name']), { id: '1', name: 'Ana' });

tests.name: a missing key is absent, not undefined (boundary)
inherited properties are never copied
the input is not modified and a new object is returned

hints: Both helpers build a fresh object. The difference is whether you walk the requested keys or the object's own keys.
For pick, walk the requested keys and copy those the object owns itself. For omit, walk the object's own keys and skip those in the excluded set.
For pick, copy a requested key only if the object itself owns it. For omit, copy every key the object owns unless it appears in the exclusion list, and in both cases leave the original object alone.

drills.title: Bug hunt: pick and omit: the runtime half of Pick and Omit
drills.instructions:
**Bug hunt.** The code in the editor is a plausible first attempt at drill 1, "pick and omit: the runtime half of Pick and Omit". It passes some of the tests, but it has one real bug, the kind a reviewer should catch before it ships.

**Your task.** Find the bug and fix it, changing as little as you can; the tests are the same as drill 1's. The spec is unchanged: Export two functions; both return a NEW object and never modify `obj`:
- `pick(obj, keys)`: only the listed keys that are OWN properties of `obj` (a listed key that is missing is simply absent from the result)
- `omit(obj, keys)`: every own enumerable property of `obj` except the listed keys

`keys` is an array of strings. Inherited properties are never copied by either function.

tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.omit, 'function', 'export omit');
assert.deepEqual(mod.omit({ id: '1', name: 'Ana', passwordHash: 'x' }, ['passwordHash']), { id: '1', name: 'Ana' });

tests.code:

tests.name: a missing key is absent, not undefined (boundary)
inherited properties are never copied
the input is not modified and a new object is returned

drills.explanation:
`k in obj` is true for inherited properties too, so `pick` copies a prototype's `role: 'admin'` into a fresh plain object, where it becomes an own, serialisable field. `Object.hasOwn(obj, k)` copies only the object's own data; `omit` was already right because `Object.keys` lists own keys only.

Only "inherited properties are never copied" fails on the starter. Every other test uses plain object literals with nothing on the prototype that matches a requested key, where `in` and `Object.hasOwn` agree. Use `Object.hasOwn` rather than `obj.hasOwnProperty(k)`: an object made with `Object.create(null)` has no such method, and the call throws a TypeError.
hints: Make an object whose prototype holds a role of admin and whose own keys do not, then pick role from it.
The in operator also finds properties on the prototype chain.
Copy a listed key only when the object owns it.
